THOUGHT: The patient has new-onset nasal and ocular dryness starting after a workplace facial/skull injury 1 month ago, with crusting and scant nasal secretions and a positive Schirmer test on the left (reduced tear production). CT shows bilateral comminuted sphenoid sinus fractures with disruption of the left vidian (pterygoid) canal. The vidian nerve carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (via the pterygopalatine ganglion) to the lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa; disruption of the vidian canal is therefore expected to produce ipsilateral decreased lacrimation and nasal gland secretion (xerophthalmia and dry nasal mucosa with crusting). Epistaxis after crust picking and nasal vestibular excoriations are secondary to mucosal dryness and crusting. The right corneal lacerations/abrasions likely reflect the traumatic event or secondary exposure, and Schirmer is unreliable on that side. Together, the history, focal imaging abnormality (left vidian canal disruption), and unilateral objective reduction in tear production make a post-traumatic vidian/pterygopalatine-parasympathetic injury the most likely diagnosis. Alternative diagnoses include primary or secondary atrophic rhinitis from mucosal loss, autoimmune dry-eye disease (Sjögren) — less likely given timing and unilateral findings — chronic rhinosinusitis with mucosal atrophy, and medication- or systemic disease–induced dryness.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Post‑traumatic injury to the left vidian (pterygoid) canal / pterygopalatine ganglion — parasympathetic denervation causing ipsilateral lacrimal and nasal gland hyposecretion (neurogenic dry eye and rhinitis sicca)
2. Secondary (post‑traumatic) atrophic rhinitis / nasal mucosal atrophy with crusting
3. Sjögren syndrome (autoimmune keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerorhinia) — less likely given acute post‑traumatic onset and unilateral Schirmer abnormality
4. Chronic rhinosinusitis with mucosal atrophy and crusting (posttraumatic change or infection)
5. Medication- or systemic disease–induced mucosal and lacrimal hyposecretion (anticholinergics, diabetes, etc.)
